activities.anchor: turn this into a checklist per component
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the triad that keeps priorities honest
activities.name: secTriadCloze

config.text: The %%0%% triad keeps the priorities honest: %%1%% (who can see), %%2%% (nothing silently altered), availability (up when needed). A 'secure' system that is down, or silently corrupts its data, has failed two of %%3%%.
config.hint: Name the three properties, then test any claim of 'secure' against all of them.

activities.anchor: It seems reasonable because that is exactly how the products are marketed
activities.caption: true or false — what security actually is
activities.name: secProductJudge

statements.s: The attacker needs one weakness, once; the defender needs every weakness closed, always.
statements.why: Asymmetric by construction — which is why security is a process, not a purchase.

statements.s: A firewall or antivirus box, once bought, makes an organisation secure.
statements.why: No single device closes every door forever — the firewall's own ports are part of the attack surface.

statements.s: Defenders who patch fast and delete whole attack classes are in practice safe from most adversaries.
statements.why: Attackers optimise effort per victim — refuse to be the lowest-hanging fruit and the economics turn your way.

statements.s: Kerckhoffs's principle says secrecy should live in the design, not the key.
statements.why: The reverse: assume the attacker knows the system; secrecy lives only in the key — and in your design, framework and stack overflow answers too.

activities.caption: call the cost of one password check
activities.name: secKdfEst

config.prompt: The professional stack tunes its password-checking so one verification takes roughly how long?
config.why: ~100 ms — imperceptible at login; devastating at scale, where each guess costs milliseconds instead of nanoseconds.
config.context: Fast GPU-verifiable hashes fall in minutes; pricing each guess is the whole game.

activities.caption: file each item by the layer it defends
activities.name: secLayerSort

config.prompt: Two layers, one catalogue — file each item:

items.label: an urgent request that beats most walls
a poisoned dependency — the 2024 xz-utils backdoor attempt

config.why: Phishing beats firewalls; patching beats ransomware — and keeping every account's access small shrinks the blast radius of whatever gets through.

activities.anchor: is then a drilled procedure, not an improv
activities.caption: assume breach — walk the response
activities.name: secIncidentBranch

config.root: The intrusion happened yesterday; overnight logs show an unfamiliar login on a VPN account. Walk the response.

choices.label: Contain — cut the account's access and segment the network
choices.feedback: Contain first: every minute of dwell time is lateral movement.

choices.label: Erase the affected servers and move on
choices.feedback: Eradication before containment invites re-entry — the attacker still holds other footholds.

choices.label: Eradicate, recover, then a blameless post-mortem
choices.feedback: The rehearsed sequence: contain, eradicate, recover — and the post-mortem fixes the system, not the person.

choices.label: Find who clicked the phishing link and fire them
choices.feedback: Blame guarantees the next breach goes unreported — the post-mortem's first rule is that it is blameless.

erase.text: Eradication before containment invites re-entry — the attacker still holds other footholds, and the logs you wiped were your map.

postmortem.text: Rehearsed, not improvised: contain, eradicate, recover, then fix the system — the drill is why Saturday runs calm.

blame.text: Blame guarantees the next breach goes unreported — the post-mortem is blameless by design.

config.why: Assume breach, make it visible, and rehearse the whole thing: contain, eradicate, recover, learn.

activities.anchor: Assemble the pieces on one generic incident
activities.caption: put the breach chain in order
activities.name: secChainOrder

config.prompt: The shape of most real ransomware cases — put the chain in order:
items: Monday: a plausible invoice email — the credential-harvesting link (phishing)
The reused password, with no second factor, yields a real login (credential stuffing)
The VPN account still reaches a file share no one revokes (excessive access)
Saturday: ransomware detonates across the share — and the backups are reachable from the same credentials
config.why: No single control stops the chain — the defences cut its links.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — crypto misused
activities.name: secSideSpot

config.prompt: One of these crypto claims is backwards — click it:
lines: AES-ECB encrypts identical blocks to identical ciphertext — the test image still shows a penguin.
Reusing a GCM nonce cancels the keystream, leaking the XOR of two plaintexts.
'I'll XOR with a secret key twice for safety' — combinatorial intuition fails at crypto design.
A comparison loop that returns early on the first mismatched character is the safe way to check tokens.
Reviewed, standard constructions and libraries beat every homemade design.
config.correction: Early return IS the leak: timing lets an attacker measure their way to a valid token character by character — the fix is constant-time comparison.
config.why: The implementation, not the mathematics, is the attack surface.

activities.caption: pair each surface with its category and matched control
activities.name: secStrideMatch

config.prompt: Pair each surface with its category and matched control:

pairs.right: spoofing — credential attacks; answered by MFA and rate limiting
tampering — a 'photo' that is a webshell; type validation, separate origin
spoofing — account recovery is the side door; expiring, single-use, entropy-heavy tokens
elevation of privilege — role checks server-side, never hidden buttons alone

config.why: Twenty minutes of this finds the misconfigurations breach reports find every month — because most breaches are not exotic; they are unmodelled.
